key_insight: This paper studies how efficient first-price auctions are for allocating prompts in agentic AI markets. It characterizes the price of anarchy: how much social welfare can be lost when independent AI agents bid strategically rather than coordinate perfectly.
problem_solved: The paper addresses prompt allocation in decentralized serving-time markets where multiple AI agents compete for each user query. It asks whether simple first-price auctions can reliably assign prompts while preserving efficiency despite private values, inference costs, and strategic bidding.
method: Model each agent’s bid as its expected value for a prompt: expected reward from the response minus inference cost.
Analyze first-price auctions as the allocation mechanism for prompts in a decentralized agentic market.
Derive price-of-anarchy bounds to quantify worst-case welfare loss from strategic behavior.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this provides theory for building scalable, transparent prompt marketplaces without needing a central controller to know each model’s capabilities or costs. It helps system designers anticipate efficiency losses and choose auction rules that better balance incentive compatibility and performance.
visual_elements: Flow diagram of a user prompt entering an agentic market with multiple bidding agents
Auction graphic showing highest bid winning and paying its own bid
Price of anarchy chart comparing optimal welfare vs. equilibrium welfare
Icon set for reward, inference cost, and prompt allocation
paper_title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
paper_authors: Shubhendu Trivedi, Jacob Eisenstein, Alekh Agarwal, Ian Gemp, Michael Kaisers
